title: C Programming Fundamentals
description: Master C programming from Zero to Advanced across 15 comprehensive modules covering basic I/O, operators, control flow, loops, patterns, functions, recursion, 1D & 2D arrays, strings, pointers, DMA, structures, file handling, preprocessors, and data structures.

modules.title: C Basics and Input/Output
modules.topics: structure of a C program, `printf`, `scanf`, data types, `sizeof`, variables, format specifiers, basic arithmetic.

modules.title: Operators and Expressions
modules.topics: arithmetic operators, increment/decrement, relational and logical operators, ternary operator, type casting, bitwise operators, operator precedence.

modules.title: Conditional Statements
modules.topics: `if`, `if-else`, `else if` ladder, nested `if`, `switch-case`, logical conditions, input validation.

modules.title: Loops
modules.topics: `for`, `while`, `do-while`, loop counters and accumulators, digit extraction, `break` and `continue`.

modules.title: Pattern Printing and Number Programs
modules.topics: nested loops, row/column logic, spaces and stars, number patterns, Pascal's triangle, Armstrong, perfect and prime numbers.

modules.title: Functions and Recursion
modules.topics: function declaration/definition/call, return values, call by value, recursion, base case and recursive case, multiple return via pointers (preview), classic recursive algorithms.

modules.title: Arrays (1D)
modules.topics: array declaration and input, traversal, searching, sorting basics, rotation, merging, frequency counting.

modules.title: 2D Arrays and Matrices
modules.topics: 2D array declaration and input, matrix arithmetic, transpose, row/column/diagonal sums, symmetry, spiral traversal, rotation, saddle points.

modules.title: Strings
modules.topics: character arrays, the null terminator, manual string operations (without `<string.h>` where specified), case conversion, anagrams, word counting.

modules.title: Pointers
modules.topics: pointer declaration, address-of and dereference operators, call by reference, pointer arithmetic, pointer-to-pointer, pointers with arrays and strings, function pointers.

modules.title: Dynamic Memory Allocation
modules.topics: `malloc`, `calloc`, `realloc`, `free`, dynamic 1D and 2D arrays, dynamic strings, memory leaks, resizable structures.

modules.title: Structures, Unions and Enums
modules.topics: `struct` declaration and usage, arrays of structures, nested structures, passing structures to functions, `union`, `enum`, `typedef`.

modules.title: File Handling
modules.topics: `fopen`/`fclose`, text file read/write/append, character/word/line counting, copying and merging files, search-and-replace, binary file I/O with structures, `fseek`/`ftell`/`rewind`.

modules.title: Preprocessor, Storage Classes and Bit Manipulation
modules.topics: `#define` macros, conditional compilation, `auto`/`static`/`extern`/`register`, `static` variables inside functions, command-line arguments, bit counting and manipulation.

modules.title: Data Structures, Algorithms and Final Project
modules.topics: singly linked lists, stacks, queues, sorting algorithms, binary search, binary search trees, and a final menu-driven project combining structures and file handling.

- If `D < 0`: two complex roots, `real ± imaginary i`, where real = `-b / 2a` and imaginary = `√(-D) / 2a`.

- `D < 0`:
```
Roots are complex
Root1 = <real> + <imag>i
Root2 = <real> - <imag>i
```

1 -5 6

Roots are real and different

Root2 = 2.00

questions.description: Read a non-negative integer and count how many bits are set to `1` in its binary representation.

questions.description: Read a positive integer and check whether it is a power of 2 (1, 2, 4, 8, 16, ...), using a bitwise trick rather than a loop of repeated division.

questions.description:
Implement a circular queue of integers using a fixed-size array of capacity 5. Support commands, one per line, until `EXIT`:
- `ENQUEUE value` — add to the rear; print `Queue Full` if it is already at capacity
- `DEQUEUE` — remove from the front, print the removed value, or `Queue Empty`
- `DISPLAY` — print all current elements from front to rear, space-separated, or `Queue Empty`
- `EXIT`

questions.outputFormat: Output from `ENQUEUE` (only on full), `DEQUEUE` and `DISPLAY`, in order.

Input:

ENQUEUE 2
ENQUEUE 3
DEQUEUE
ENQUEUE 4
DISPLAY
EXIT

Output:
1
2 3 4
questions.hint: Use `front`, `rear` and `count` (not just front/rear) to distinguish "full" from "empty" cleanly. Advance indices with wraparound: `rear = (rear + 1) % capacity;`. questions.description: Read `n` integers into an array and sort it using **either** quick sort or merge sort (your choice), implemented recursively. Print the sorted array.
questions.hint: Merge sort: split into two halves, sort each recursively, merge (reuse the merge logic from Module 7, Question 9). Quick sort: pick a pivot, partition the array around it, then recursively sort each side. Merge sort is more predictable for large `n` (guaranteed O(n log n)); quick sort's worst case is O(n²) on already-sorted or adversarial input.

questions.description:
Implement a Binary Search Tree (BST) of integers. Support commands, one per line, until `EXIT`:
- `INSERT value` — insert into the BST (ignore duplicates silently — do not insert them again)
- `SEARCH value` — print `Found` or `Not Found`
- `INORDER` — print all values via inorder traversal (which visits them in sorted order), space-separated, or `Empty tree`
- `EXIT`
questions.inputFormat: A sequence of commands ending with `EXIT`.
questions.example:
Input:
INSERT 50
INSERT 30
INSERT 70
INSERT 20
INORDER
SEARCH 30
SEARCH 99
EXIT

Output:
20 30 50 70
Found
Not Found
questions.hint: In `struct Node { int data; struct Node *left, *right; };`, `insert` recursively compares the new value with the current node: smaller goes left, larger goes right, equal is ignored. `inorder` recursively visits left, prints the node, visits right — this visiting order is exactly what produces sorted output.

questions.description:
Build a menu-driven Bank Management System combining structures and file handling. Store accounts in a binary file `accounts.dat` using `struct Account { int accNo; char name[50]; double balance; };`. Support commands, one per line, until `EXIT`:
- `CREATE accNo name initialBalance` — create a new account; print `Account created` or `Account already exists`
- `DEPOSIT accNo amount` — add to balance; print `New balance: <value>` (2 decimals) or `Account not found`
- `WITHDRAW accNo amount` — subtract from balance if sufficient funds; print `New balance: <value>`, or `Insufficient funds`, or `Account not found`
- `BALANCE accNo` — print `Balance: <value>` or `Account not found`
- `TRANSFER fromAcc toAcc amount` — withdraw from one account and deposit into another, only if both exist and funds are sufficient; print `Transfer successful`, or the specific failure reason
- `LIST` — print all accounts as `accNo name balance` (2 decimals), ordered by account number ascending, or `No accounts`
- `EXIT`
questions.inputFormat: A sequence of commands, one per line, ending with `EXIT`.
questions.outputFormat: Output from every command except `CREATE` on success and `EXIT`, in the order given. (`CREATE` does print its own message too — see the command list above.)
questions.constraints: Account numbers are unique positive integers; amounts are positive with up to 2 decimal places; up to 1000 accounts.
questions.example:
Input:
CREATE 101 Aarav 5000
CREATE 102 Priya 3000
DEPOSIT 101 1000
WITHDRAW 102 5000
TRANSFER 101 102 2000
BALANCE 101
BALANCE 102
LIST
EXIT

Output:
Account created
Account created
New balance: 6000.00
Insufficient funds
Transfer successful
Balance: 4000.00
Balance: 5000.00
101 Aarav 4000.00
102 Priya 5000.00
questions.hint: As in Module 13 Question 10, the simplest reliable approach is to load all accounts into memory (an array or a sorted structure) at the start, perform every operation on that in-memory copy, and rewrite the entire `accounts.dat` file after each change (or once at the very end, before `EXIT`, if your grading only checks the final file state). Keep the accounts sorted by `accNo` (or sort just before `LIST`) to satisfy the ascending-order requirement.
